questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: An integral with no elementary antiderivative
questions.learningObjective: recognise which integrand cannot be integrated in elementary terms
questions.stem: Four definite integrals are listed below. Which one has no antiderivative that can be written in terms of finite combinations of the usual functions?

options.text: The integral from 0 to 1 of the exponential of minus x squared, with respect to x
The integral from 0 to 1 of the cube of x, with respect to x
options.misconception: treats a power of x as though it hid a non-elementary integrand

options.text: The integral from 0 to 1 of 1 divided by 1 plus x squared, with respect to x
options.misconception: believes a quadratic denominator rules out an elementary antiderivative

options.text: The integral from 0 to 1 of the square root of 1 plus x squared, with respect to x
options.misconception: confuses a radical integrand with one that has no elementary antiderivative

questions.explanation: The exponential of minus x squared is the standard example. Substituting u equal to x squared leaves the square root of u in the denominator, so no substitution ever clears it, and the antiderivative has to be named rather than computed. The other three are all elementary: the cube of x integrates to a power, 1 divided by 1 plus x squared integrates to the arctangent, and the square root of 1 plus x squared integrates by a hyperbolic substitution. The exponential of a square is special because the derivative of x squared brings its own square root along.
questions.hint: Try a substitution on each integrand and see which one leaves a square root in the denominator.

questions.learningObjective: report the value of an integral with no elementary antiderivative
questions.stem: Give the value of the integral from 0 to 1 of the exponential of minus x squared, with respect to x, to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: The antiderivative has to be named, since no elementary expression exists, and the accepted one is the square root of pi times 2 times the error function evaluated at 1. Evaluating that gives 0.7468241328, which rounds to 0.746824 at six decimal places. The same figure comes out of high-precision numerical quadrature, and the two agree to fourteen decimal places, which is the check that the named function and the quadrature are computing the same quantity. The integrand is positive and below 1 on the whole interval, so a value between 0 and 1 is the only sensible shape for the answer.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Why a closed form is missing
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing why a substitution cannot produce an elementary antiderivative
questions.stem: Explain in a few sentences why no substitution turns the integral of the exponential of minus x squared into an elementary expression.

answer.exemplar: The obvious substitution u equal to x squared needs a factor of 2 times the square root of u in the numerator, and the resulting integral of the exponential of minus u over the square root of u has no elementary antiderivative either, so the radical that would be needed to undo the substitution never disappears.

questions.explanation: A substitution succeeds when the new variable appears with constant differential and no leftover radical. Here the chain rule factor is 2x, so using u equal to x squared leaves the integrand as the exponential of minus u divided by 2 times the square root of u, and the square root of u is exactly what blocks the elementary exponential integral. Any other substitution simply relocates the same square root, which is why the antiderivative has to be given a name instead of a formula. The practical consequence is that the integral is computed numerically, and the numerical methods are built to be checked against each other rather than against a closed form.
questions.hint: Look at the chain rule factor that the natural substitution introduces and ask what it leaves behind.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: state what a quadrature estimate does and does not claim
questions.stem: A numerical method returns a single number for a definite integral. What is the honest description of what that number is?

options.text: The exact value of the integral, computed in a different but equally valid notation
options.misconception: claims that a numerical route recovers the exact value of the integral

options.text: A value that is exact whenever the integrand is continuous on the closed interval
options.misconception: believes continuity alone makes a numerical result exact

options.text: A value whose digits are trustworthy to the full precision printed on the display
options.misconception: assumes that digits shown by the machine are digits that are correct

options.text: An approximation whose accuracy is governed by a rule that can be checked and improved

questions.explanation: A quadrature rule replaces the integral by a finite weighted sum of function values, and the difference between the two is controlled by the behaviour of the integrand, not by the number of digits displayed. That control is what makes the method usable: the error can be bounded, the bound can be turned into a required number of panels, and doubling the panel count reduces the error by a known factor. Continuity guarantees the integral exists, which is a different statement, and the number of printed digits reflects the arithmetic rather than the accuracy.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the error when the panel width is halved.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: predict whether the trapezoid rule overestimates or underestimates
questions.stem: The integrand on an interval has a positive second derivative everywhere, so the curve is convex. How does the composite trapezoid rule compare with the true value of the integral?

options.text: It agrees exactly, because the rule already accounts for the curvature of the graph
options.misconception: believes the rule fits the curve, when it replaces it by straight pieces

options.text: It has no consistent direction, because the error depends on the panel count
options.misconception: thinks changing the number of panels can flip the sign of the error

options.text: It overestimates, because each chord lies above the curve it replaces
It underestimates, because each chord lies below the curve it replaces
options.misconception: reverses the chord and curve ordering that convexity forces

questions.explanation: The trapezoid rule replaces the curve on each panel by the straight chord joining the endpoint values, and for a convex curve the chord sits above the curve throughout the interior of the panel. Each panel therefore contributes a little too much, and the errors add rather than cancel, so the total is an overestimate. The midpoint rule does the opposite, since it samples the curve itself and misses the corners where a convex curve rises above its chord. This pairing is why the two rules bracket the true value for a convex integrand.
questions.hint: Compare a chord of a convex curve with the curve on the same short panel.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Why the trapezoid rule is exact on a line
questions.learningObjective: identify the class of integrands on which the trapezoid rule is exact
questions.stem: Why is the composite trapezoid rule exact for an integrand whose graph is a straight line on the whole interval?

options.text: The chord the rule uses is then the graph itself, so nothing is approximated
The rule averages the endpoint values, which is the average rate of a linear function
options.misconception: credits the endpoint average rather than the geometry of the chord

options.text: The panel count cancels out for a linear integrand, so any count gives the same value
options.misconception: claims the panel count is irrelevant, which is true here but not the reason

options.text: A linear integrand has a zero second derivative, so the error term vanishes identically
options.misconception: invokes the error term without noticing the geometric reason

questions.explanation: The trapezoid rule computes the area of the trapezoid under each chord. When the curve is itself a straight line, that chord coincides with the curve on the panel, so the computed area is the true area panel by panel and the total is exact for any panel count. This is why the rule is used as a yardstick: it reproduces the simplest possible case exactly, so any discrepancy on a curved graph is attributable to the curve rather than to the rule. Simpson's rule extends the same idea, reproducing parabolas exactly because its weights fit a quadratic through three points.
questions.hint: Picture the region under a straight line and the trapezoid built on the same two endpoints.

questions.learningObjective: predict whether the midpoint rule overestimates or underestimates
questions.stem: The midpoint rule samples the integrand at the middle of each panel. For a convex integrand, how does the resulting estimate compare with the true value of the integral?

options.text: It overestimates, because the rectangle covers the corners the curve rises into
options.misconception: reverses the rectangle and curve ordering that convexity forces

options.text: It is exact, because the midpoint of a panel is its most representative point
options.misconception: believes a representative sample makes the rectangle rule exact

questions.learningObjective: take a secant step from two starting values
questions.stem: The secant method is applied to f of x equal to x squared minus 5, starting from the two values 2 and 3. What is the first new value it produces? Give the value as a decimal number.
questions.explanation: The secant method draws the line through the two starting points, which are (2, minus 1) and (3, 4), and takes where that line meets the horizontal axis. The slope of the line is the difference 4 minus minus 1 over 3 minus 2, that is 5, so the crossing is 3 minus 4 over 5, which is 2.2. The line's slope was estimated from the function's own chord rather than from a derivative, which is what removes the need for a derivative. The true root is 2.236068, so the step moved from a starting error of 0.236 to an error of 0.036.
questions.hint: Find the slope of the line through the two starting points, then take where it meets the axis.

questions.topic: Fixed point iteration for a square root
questions.learningObjective: iterate a self-referential formula and compare with the exact root
questions.stem: The iteration that sends x to the quantity x plus 7 over x, all divided by 2, is used to compute the square root of 7. Starting from x equal to 2, what value does it produce after two applications? Report your answer to six decimal places.

The second application replaces 2.75 by 2.75 plus 7 over 2.75, that is 2.75 plus 2.545454, which is 5.295454, all divided by 2, giving 2.647727 at six decimal places. The exact value of the square root of 7 is 2.645751, so after two steps the error is 0.001976, down from 0.645751 at the starting value. questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an iteration that never settles
questions.stem: A student iterates the rule that sends x to x squared minus 1, starting from 0, and reports the values 0, minus 1, 0, minus 1 and then declares the search finished at 0. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The values are too close together, so the student should have declared convergence earlier
options.misconception: treats two close values as evidence of convergence

options.text: The rule needs a starting value above 1 before it will produce a decreasing sequence
options.misconception: believes the starting value alone fixes the behaviour of the iteration

options.text: The rule is being applied with the wrong sign, and minus x squared plus 1 would settle
options.misconception: blames a sign error rather than the structure of the rule

options.text: The sequence alternates between 0 and minus 1 forever, so no limit is being approached

questions.explanation: Sending 0 through the rule gives minus 1, and sending minus 1 through it gives 0 again, so the sequence is 0, minus 1, 0, minus 1 with no approach to a single value. The rule has two fixed points where x equals x squared minus 1, that is 1.618034 and minus 0.618034, and a starting value of 0 lies in the basin of the two-cycle rather than in the basin of either fixed point. The diagnosis is a genuine failure to converge, and it is exactly what the mean value theorem test predicts, since the magnitude of the derivative of the rule exceeds 1 at both values in the cycle.
questions.hint: Compute the next two values after minus 1 and see whether the sequence settles anywhere.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: state the derivative condition that makes a fixed point attracting
questions.stem: An iteration sends x to g of x, and r is a fixed point of g. What condition on the derivative at r makes the iteration attract nearby starting values?

options.text: The derivative of g at r equals 0, which is needed for the error to vanish immediately
options.misconception: requires a zero slope, which is far stronger than attraction

options.text: The derivative of g at r is greater than 1, so each step amplifies the error away from r
options.misconception: states the repelling condition as though it were the attracting one

options.text: The magnitude of the derivative of g at r is less than 1, so errors shrink from step to step
The derivative of g at r is exactly 1, so each step preserves the error it started with
options.misconception: treats a unit slope as the condition for contraction

questions.explanation: The mean value theorem turns the difference between an iterate and the fixed point into the derivative at an intermediate point times the previous difference, so if the derivative stays below 1 in magnitude the difference is forced to shrink at every step and the sequence converges to the fixed point. A derivative of exactly 1 leaves the size of the difference unchanged, and a derivative above 1 pushes iterates away. The slope test is local, which is why it is a prediction about starting values near r rather than a global guarantee, and why a two-cycle can coexist with an attracting fixed point in the same rule.
questions.hint: Apply the mean value theorem between an iterate and the fixed point and read off the factor.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Checking the output of a search
questions.learningObjective: explain why a computed root must be substituted back into the equation
questions.stem: A numerical search reports a value as the solution of an equation. What check should always be run on that value before it is believed?

options.text: Confirm the derivative at the value is not zero, since zero would be a singularity
options.misconception: insists a root must be a regular point, which rules out the ones with largest multiplicity

options.text: Substitute it into the original equation and confirm the value left is small enough
Confirm the search stopped after the number of steps that was requested of it
options.misconception: treats a completed step count as evidence of accuracy

options.text: Confirm the reported value is different from every starting value used
options.misconception: demands that the answer differ from the guesses, which is not a requirement

questions.explanation: A search can stop for the wrong reason: too large a tolerance, a step that left the neighbourhood of the root, or a starting value in a two-cycle. Substituting the reported value into the original equation is the direct test, because the size of the leftover is the error in the function value rather than in the position of the root. A second useful check is to vary the starting value and see whether the answer moves, since a genuine root of a well-behaved equation is found from anywhere in its basin, while a spurious one is found only from a particular starting point.
questions.hint: Ask what a genuine root looks like when the function is evaluated at it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: estimate a derivative from two sampled function values
questions.stem: A function is sampled at the point 2 and at 2.001, giving the values 4 and 4.004001. What does the forward difference quotient give as an estimate of the derivative at the point 2? Give the value to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: The forward difference quotient is the change in the function divided by the change in the input, here 4.004001 minus 4, that is 0.004001, over 0.001, which is 4.001 at six decimal places. The exact derivative of the square of x at 2 is 4, so the estimate is high by exactly 0.001, which is the step size. That is not a coincidence: the leading error of a forward difference is the step size times half the second derivative, and the second derivative here is 2. The estimate therefore gets better only as the step shrinks.
questions.hint: Divide the difference of the two sampled values by the difference of the two inputs.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: estimate a derivative from three sampled values symmetrically
questions.stem: The same function is now sampled at 1.999 as well, where its value is 3.996001. What does the central difference quotient give for the derivative at the point 2, and how does that compare with the exact value?
questions.explanation: The central difference quotient is the value at 2.001 minus the value at 1.999, that is 4.004001 minus 3.996001, which is 0.008, over 2 times 0.001, which is 0.002, giving exactly 4. The exact derivative of the square of x at 2 is also 4, so the estimate is exact to the digits shown, and that is the point of the symmetric form: the leading error of a central difference is proportional to the square of the step times one sixth of the third derivative, and the third derivative here is 0, so the error vanishes altogether. A one-sided difference on the same data would have been high by 0.001.
questions.hint: Divide the difference of the two outer values by the distance between the two outer inputs.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Error order of the difference formulas
questions.learningObjective: compare the error order of one-sided and symmetric differences
questions.stem: How does the truncation error of a difference formula depend on the step size?

options.text: It is first order in the step for a forward difference and second order for a central difference
It is second order for a forward difference and first order for a central difference
options.misconception: swaps the two rates, giving the one-sided form the better order

options.text: It is second order for both, because the step appears squared in each formula
options.misconception: assumes the symmetric form shares the one-sided error rate

options.text: It does not depend on the step, since the step cancels from every difference quotient
options.misconception: believes the step cancels out of the error as well

questions.explanation: A forward difference keeps only one side of the secant, so the first-order term in the expansion survives and the error is the step times half the second derivative. The symmetric form averages the two one-sided estimates, and that average cancels the first-order term, leaving the step squared times one sixth of the third derivative. The difference is worth several decimal digits for a step of 0.001, which is why a symmetric difference is preferred whenever the function can be sampled on both sides of the point.
questions.hint: Expand the function at the two sampled points and see which power of the step survives in each formula.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: A step that is too small
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the loss of accuracy from an excessively small step
questions.stem: A student computes a derivative with a central difference and shrinks the step from 0.001 to 0.000000000001, and the answer gets worse. What has happened?

options.text: The function has become constant at that scale, so every difference is zero
options.misconception: believes a function can lose its variation when the sample points move closer

options.text: The step has become smaller than the interval on which the function is defined
options.misconception: believes a step cannot be smaller than the domain of the function

options.text: The central difference is only valid for steps larger than 0.000000000001
options.misconception: invents a lower limit on the usable step size

options.text: The two sampled values have become equal in the stored precision, so the quotient is dominated by rounding

questions.explanation: A difference quotient subtracts two numbers that are close together when the step is small, and a subtraction of nearly equal numbers loses most of the significant digits it started with. Meanwhile the truncation error keeps falling, so at some point the rounding error is the larger of the two and the answer stops improving and then deteriorates. The practical lesson is that the step has to be chosen, not minimised: too large and the truncation error dominates, too small and the rounding error does, and the best choice sits between them. The same trade-off appears in any computation built from a small difference.
questions.hint: Ask how many significant digits survive when two nearly equal stored values are subtracted.

questions.topic: Second difference for a second derivative
questions.learningObjective: estimate a second derivative from three sampled values
questions.stem: A function has the values 9.0601, 9 and 8.9401 at the points 3.01, 3 and 2.99. What does the symmetric second difference give as an estimate of the second derivative at the point 3?
questions.explanation: The symmetric second difference is the value at 3.01 minus twice the value at 3 plus the value at 2.99, all divided by the square of the step, that is 9.0601 minus 18 plus 8.9401, which is 0.0002, over 0.0001, giving 2. For the square of x the exact second derivative is the constant 2 at every point, so the estimate is exact, and the leading error of this formula involves the fourth derivative, which here is 0. Sampling symmetrically is what removes the first-order term, so the accuracy depends on the square of the step rather than on the step itself.

questions.topic: Numerical derivative against the exact one
questions.learningObjective: compare a numerical derivative with the exact value and judge the error
questions.stem: The sine of x is sampled at 0.499 and 0.501 and the symmetric difference quotient is formed. To nine decimal places, what value does it give for the derivative of the sine at the point 0.5, and what is the exact value there?
questions.explanation: The quotient is the sine of 0.501 minus the sine of 0.499, divided by 0.002, which is 0.877582416 to nine decimal places. The exact derivative of the sine is the cosine, and the cosine of 0.5 is 0.877582562 to nine decimal places, so the estimate is low by 0.000000146. That figure is what the error formula predicts: the square of the step over 6 times the third derivative, which is 0.000001 over 6 times the negative of the cosine of 0.5, that is minus 0.000000146. The agreement between prediction and measurement is the check that the difference formula is behaving as the theory says.
questions.hint: Form the symmetric quotient, then subtract the cosine of 0.5 to see the size of the error.
